items_missed: No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. This is a $5,500 to $12,500 two-day interstate-distance move carrying a 300-pound petrified tree stump, a washer and dryer, and a full primary bedroom set, spending a night loaded in a truck in another city — and the customer never heard that it carries up to $2,000 to repair, replace or reimburse. On a long-haul move the damage question is the one every customer is privately holding, and it was never answered.

Meet Your Mover never mentioned. On a two-day move where a crew spends the night away and comes back to the customer's new home the following morning, knowing who those people are is worth more than on any other call this week.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned, despite both arrival windows being stated ('both days we'd be looking at an arrival between 8:30 AM and 9:00 AM').

Walk distance never asked at either address. He asked about access obstacles at the destination — 'any special notes about the access there that would slow us down like low hanging tree limbs narrow doorways and pin driveways' — but never how far the truck sits from the door at either end, on a job where he is pricing eleven and a half hours of crew time.

No equivalents or plain-language anchors used anywhere. On a quote that started at $12,464, giving the customer a way to picture the load would have surfaced the square-footage problem before the customer had to.

The estimate was built on a square footage the customer had already told him was wrong. 'I put in goofy stuff because I didn't want it to spit out an inaccurate quote. My, all of my kids have moved out and we got rid of everything on the second floor... We're using like four rooms nowadays.' Khevan heard it and even restated it — 'so it's kind of a 2500 square foot equivalent out of the larger home' — and then built the quote off 2500 square feet anyway, six movers on two trucks, $12,464.

No deposit required never mentioned. This is the highest-cost miss in the booking section. The customer had visible sticker shock — 'that's a lot more money than I even. What I guess that's like double what I would have even guessed' — and 'there's no deposit and no card on file, so I can hold both days for you at no cost while you send the video' is the exact bridge from shock to a held date. It was never said, and the move ended the call unbooked.

No booking re-attempt after the corrected quote. He asked once, before the objection — 'If you wanted to save the spots then we absolutely have that availability' — and after cutting the number by more than half to $5,519, he never asked again. The customer's reaction to the revised figure was 'That would have been my guess. I was guessing under six,' which is agreement, and nobody moved to close on it.

No 'reply with any corrections' verification ask. The reply request he made is a process ping, not a verification: 'once you do get that, would you mind just shooting us a quick text or responding? So I'll send over the estimate email... And then if you just want to respond to that email just let us know you've submitted it.' That asks the customer to confirm he did a task, not to check whether the captured details are right — on a call that captured two addresses, a two-day schedule, a packing scope and three separate fee structures.
BOLDED key details at the top of the email never mentioned.
No 'any other questions before I let you go?' The call closed on 'Of course, I appreciate you taking the time.'
Hours never given. The callback path was 'shoot us a text' to a number, with no indication of when anyone would answer.
Customer's name used once — 'Andrew, how's up? What's up?' — short of the 3+ standard across a fifteen-minute call, and notable because the customer had just said he goes by Drew on the email.
Effective insurance explanation missed entirely — no No Worries, no 60¢/lb baseline, no mention of coverage in any form on the most valuable move in this week's sample.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10, on the call where it was worth the most money in the whole batch. At $109 per mover per hour with six movers on day one, an hour of prep saved is roughly $654. The customer is actively downsizing, said 'we've just gotten rid of so much stuff,' and is packing only the kitchen and some closets — a consolidation and carload speech would have landed on a receptive audience and made a real dent in an eleven-and-a-half-hour day one.
top_strength: Khevan runs the best discovery in this week's sample — a clean 9/9 on probe, the only one in the batch — and he opens with the textbook agenda: 'I will start with making sure I've got all the details then we'll jump into the pricing structure. And then hopefully by the end we can get a good estimate for you and find a spot on our schedule. How's that sound?' Roadmap, outcome, confirmation, all in one sentence. From there he covered every probe bullet that applied: special considerations with concrete categories ('antique furniture, gun safe home gym equipment, anything like that') which surfaced the 300-pound petrified tree stump, followed immediately by the operationally relevant follow-up ('Is it going ground floor to ground floor?'); packing scope ('are we going to be packing up the entirety of the home, or was it just a few items or specific rooms'); additional stops; destination access with specifics most reps never ask ('low hanging tree limbs narrow doorways and pin driveways'); and the moving-stressor question by name — 'do you have any specific stressor or concerns about the moving process in general' — which almost nobody in this sample asks. His fee transparency on the hardest-to-explain structure in the batch is genuinely strong. He separated the three out-of-hourly items cleanly, gave each a stated reason rather than just a number — the $240 per truck 'covers the cost of our crew staying the night in a city that is not our kind of home base,' the $1,800 per truck 'covers the cost of getting our empty truck and crew back' — and then denied fees with the customer's own item named back to him: 'there are no fees for the petrified tree stump and table, for anything that's going to be disassembled or reassembled, no fees for booking cancellation and no fees of any type.' But the best moment on the call is the recovery. When the customer pushed back — 'that's a lot more money than I even... that's like double what I would have even guessed it would be to do this and I'm not saying wrong, I'm just maybe I'm uninformed' — Khevan did not defend the number and did not discount it. He owned the error out loud: 'yeah, so I've, you know, I probably trusted the square footage a little too much there.' Then he rebuilt the quote live at the right crew size ('$5,519, that's two guys on day one, about twelve hours and then two guys on day two about four'), offered two walkthrough formats so the customer could pick, and closed the loop with a thoughtful touch — 'I'll send it on the two guys one truck estimate as well, so it's not as jarring.' A rep who admits the estimate was wrong, fixes it in real time, and manages the customer's experience of reading the email afterwards is a rep worth investing in. The rapport was real too: the empty-nest exchange ('It's so weird being in this house without the kids' → 'I am just starting the first half of that journey... So I'll know what that's like here in eighteen or twenty years') earned a 'Oh, nice congratulations,' and the call ended on 'Very nice. Outstanding.'
coaching_note: Estimate-accuracy flag, and this is the headline of the week — it belongs in the bottom-4 review conversation even though it is a process failure rather than a judgment failure. Khevan quoted $12,464 and then re-quoted $5,519 on the same call, a 56% reduction, using information he already had before he built the first number. The customer told him at minute two: 'I put in goofy stuff because I didn't want it to spit out an inaccurate quote... all of my kids have moved out and we got rid of everything on the second floor. We're using like four rooms nowadays.' Khevan acknowledged it — 'so it's kind of a 2500 square foot equivalent out of the larger home' — and then went to the 2500 sqft playbook anyway: five to six movers, two trucks, seven to eight hours locally. His own words at the end name the failure exactly: 'I probably trusted the square footage a little too much there.' The lesson is not that he padded to be safe — it is that he took a form field over a live customer statement. When a customer tells you the square footage overstates the load, the square footage is dead and the room-by-room inventory is the input. He already had that inventory: living room, study equivalent, formal dining, kitchen nook and chairs, bar stools, primary bedroom with two bedside tables, dresser and bed, two small desks and a mattress upstairs, two outdoor couch sets and chairs, washer and dryer, and a garage with bicycles. That is a two-bedroom load and the customer said so — 'I don't think we have more stuff than you would find in like a two bedroom home.' The fix is a single habit: when the inventory and the square footage disagree, say so out loud and size off the inventory. 'You've described about a two-bedroom load in a 2500 square foot shell, so I'm going to size this off what you've actually got rather than the square footage — two movers, one truck.' Also worth flagging for Amanda: the $6,945 swing happened because the customer pushed back. A customer who did not push would have received a $12,464 estimate, and either booked it and been overcharged for crew he did not need, or walked. That is the accuracy problem's commercial cost in one transaction. Second priority: the move is not booked. Khevan asked once, before the objection, and never again after he fixed the number. The customer's response to $5,519 was 'That would have been my guess. I was guessing under six' — agreement — and the call ended with a video homework assignment and no date held. The close he needed: 'That sounds a lot closer to what you had in mind. Here's what I'd do — there's no deposit and no card to hold a date, so let me pencil both days in for you right now while you get that video over. It costs you nothing, and if the walkthrough moves the number either direction we adjust before you pay anything. What dates are you targeting?' That is the booking attempt plus the no-deposit differentiator, and it converts a homework assignment into a held slot. Third, the three differentiators are all missing on the most expensive move in the sample. No Worries Damage Coverage on a 300-pound petrified stump and a truck sitting loaded overnight in another city is not a nice-to-have; it is the answer to the question the customer has not asked. Meet Your Mover on a two-day job where the same crew sleeps over and comes back the next morning is unusually reassuring. And the On-Time Guarantee costs eight words after stating the 8:30-to-9:00 window. Fourth, the Save Your Ass speech is worth more here than on any other call this week — six movers at $109 an hour means an hour of customer prep is roughly $654 back in his pocket, and he is a downsizer who is already in the mood to purge.
phone_presence_notes: Easy, genuine rapport from a recovery most reps would have fumbled — after the accidental 'Yo,' he explained himself without defensiveness ('I apologize for the informality you sounded a lot like an Andrew') and the customer laughed it off into a Breaking Bad riff — followed by a real human exchange when the customer got wistful about the empty house ('I am just starting the first half of that journey... So I'll know what that's like here in eighteen or twenty years' → 'Oh, nice congratulations'), and a non-defensive, ego-free ownership of a $7,000 estimate error that left the customer saying 'Very nice. Outstanding.'
